name: NJ-12
label: Safe D

key_factors: District's D+13 partisan lean in an open-seat race
Hamawy's roughly 20-to-1 fundraising edge plus nearly $1.9 million in outside support
Prediction markets price Democratic victory near 98 percent
No public polling or expert ratings, leaving fundamentals to carry the forecast
model.rationale: The district's thirteen-point Democratic lean, Adam Hamawy's roughly twenty-to-one fundraising advantage over Gregg Mele, and prediction markets pricing a Democratic win near 98 percent all point to a comfortable hold despite the open seat.
model.watch: A late wave of Republican outside spending or any polling showing a single-digit race would be the main reason to revisit this outlook.
notes: No expert rater lists this race; treated as safe for the party holding the seat.
No usable general-election polls; forecast rests on fundamentals and expert ratings.
Open seat: Bonnie Watson Coleman (D) is not on the ballot.

overview:
New Jersey's 12th District sits firmly in Democratic territory, with a partisan lean of about thirteen points. The open-seat contest to succeed retiring Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman features Democrat Adam Hamawy against Republican Gregg Mele, with minor-party candidates also on the ballot. No public polls or outside expert ratings cover this race, so the outlook rests on district fundamentals, campaign finance, and betting markets.

Hamawy has raised roughly $1.9 million and drawn nearly as much in outside support, while Mele has raised under $100,000 with about $10,000 left in cash. Prediction markets put Democratic chances near 98 percent. The combination of a strongly Democratic district, a large financial edge, and market pricing points to a comfortable Democratic hold, with the main uncertainty coming from the absence of polling in an open-seat contest.
